## Paper 2 · Session 03 · Soil water, from a simple regression {.center .scrollable}

## The paper, and its question {.scrollable}

**Amsili, van Es & Schindelbeck (2024)**, *Pedotransfer functions for field capacity, permanent
wilting point, and available water capacity based on random forest modeling*, Communications in
Soil Science and Plant Analysis · [article](https://doi.org/10.1080/00103624.2024.2336573)

Measuring how much water a soil holds takes a laboratory. The authors predict it from cheap,
routine measurements — sand, clay, organic matter — with a random forest, and report a linear
regression with product terms alongside it.

> **Can cheap, routinely measured soil properties predict a soil's water-holding capacity well
> enough to replace direct measurement — and does a random forest do better than a regression?**

## The data, and the simple model {.scrollable}

**One row = one topsoil sample** sent to the Cornell lab, 2015–2019 · 7,232 soils · field capacity
in g of water per g of soil; sand, clay and organic matter (SOM) in %.

## What you should find {.scrollable}

| | adj. $R^2$ |
|---|---|
| Ours · sand + clay + SOM | **0.786** |
| Ours · + SOM squared (AIC −24603 → −24612) | 0.786 |
| Paper · + three pairwise products | 0.79 |
| Paper · full random forest (% variance, out-of-bag) | 0.86 |

::: {.check}
**In words:** one more point of organic matter goes with **0.024 g/g** more water held; ten more
points of sand with **0.025 g/g** less. Row 5986 — a clay soil holding 0.09 g/g where the model
expects 0.355 — has the largest Cook's distance, but dropping it moves no slope.
:::

## What it does not license {.scrollable}

::: {.tight}
- **No causal claim.** A pattern across one lab's soils, not what adding organic matter to a field
  would do.
- **No out-of-sample claim.** Our $R^2$ is in-sample; the paper's forest scores are out-of-bag —
  not the same yardstick.
- **No claim beyond the sampled soils** — US topsoils, organic matter capped at 10%. And row 5986
  is to be checked, not deleted.
:::
